transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess the main reason I finally made this appointment—and my wife has been gently nudging me to do this for a while now, honestly—is because of how things are going at work. I'm a medical services manager, so I oversee operations for a few different outpatient clinics. It's a busy job, which is usually fine when I'm walking the floor, talking to the staff, or putting out sudden fires. I'm actually pretty good at the fast-paced stuff. 

But the problem is... well, anytime I have to do something that takes real, sustained, sitting-down brain work, I just absolutely hit a wall. Like, I have these monthly compliance and budget reports. I know how to do them, I have my degree in healthcare admin, I know the drill inside and out. But I will sit down at my desk, open the spreadsheet, and it's like my brain just refuses to engage. Or, as another example, right now we're in the middle of planning this big multi-site health screening event for the community. The logistics for it require a lot of deep focus to map out the staff rotations, the supply chains, the permits, all of that. And I just keep putting it off. 

I'll find a hundred other little things to do instead, like checking the glove inventory or answering emails that really aren't urgent, even though I know this event planning is the absolute most critical thing on my plate right now. It's just so incredibly draining to even think about starting the heavy mental lifting, so I end up pushing it to the very last minute. It stresses everyone out, especially me, and I just don't understand why I can't just sit and do the work when I know exactly how much it matters.

Have you noticed this kind of difficulty getting started on demanding, detail-heavy tasks going back to your school days or early adulthood, or is this something that's really only become a problem recently?

Oh, it’s definitely not a new thing, not at all. I mean, if I really sit back and think about it—and my wife and I were actually just talking about this the other night after I spent three hours avoiding a budget reconciliation—it goes way, way back. All the way back to elementary school, honestly. I remember my parents having these parent-teacher conferences, and it was always the exact same story, year after year. The teachers would sit there in those tiny little chairs and tell my mom and dad, "You know, he’s a bright kid, he really is, he’s got a lot of potential." But then came the "but." It was always, "But he’s constantly daydreaming, staring out the window, totally in his own world." 

And the worksheets! Oh man, the amount of lost worksheets. I would do them—well, sometimes I’d do them—and then they would just vanish into the black hole of my desk or my backpack. I’d get all the way to school, and the teacher would ask for the homework, and I’d just have this sinking feeling because I knew I didn’t have it, even though I could picture myself sitting at the kitchen table looking at it the night before. 

Honestly, the only reason I ever passed anything back then was because my mother was basically my personal assistant. Every single night, without fail, she would stand there in the kitchen, grab my backpack, and physically pull everything out. She’d check off what was done, what was missing, and make sure I actually put the finished stuff back in a specific folder so I could hand it in. If she hadn't done that, I don't think I would have turned in a single assignment. And it’s funny, because even when I got to college for my associate's degree, I still struggled with that same feeling of just... not being able to corral my brain when it came to the dense, boring stuff. So yeah, this isn't just a recent work thing, it’s been the story of my life for as long as I can remember. It’s just that now, instead of a lost math worksheet, it’s a lost supply chain manifest, you know?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong pattern of difficulty sustaining attention on tasks requiring deep, detailed mental effort, avoidance/procrastination of effortful cognitive tasks, forgetfulness (losing worksheets, needing external organizational support), and distractibility (daydreaming, off-task behavior) documented consistently from elementary school through adulthood. These symptoms are present across settings (school, college, and current workplace) and have caused functional impairment (near-failure academically without maternal intervention; current occupational stress and last-minute task completion). The chronicity (childhood onset, persisting >6 months, indeed lifelong), pervasiveness across contexts, and predominance of inattentive-type symptoms without described hyperactive-impulsive symptoms support a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
